My doctor submitted two prescriptions for the same medication for different cycles, but I only needed one. When I logged into Alto’s portal, I selected and approved what I understood to be the most recent prescription, which had a cost of approximately $1,000. I entered my credit card information specifically to approve that prescription. I didn’t take a screenshot of this since I figured everything was OK.

To my surprise, Alto processed and charged me for both prescriptions, resulting in nearly $2,000 in charges. I only discovered this after seeing the charge on my credit card.

When I contacted customer service, I was told that both medications had already been shipped and that nothing could be done. I escalated the issue to supervisors, hoping for a resolution, but was met with little empathy and no meaningful assistance. They asked me for proof of what I agreed to pay for and of course, I didn’t have it, I only had the 2K charge on my credit card.

As a result, I was charged roughly over $1,000 for medication I did not need and did not intend to use and order. The entire experience was frustrating, expensive, and extremely disappointing.

To make matters worse, after this happened, I contacted my insurance company to understand what went wrong. According to the representative I spoke with, I should avoid using this pharmacy in the future because they said Alto processes medications as cash-pay transactions in situations where insurance coverage may have significantly reduced the cost. Had I known this beforehand, I would never have used this pharmacy.

Between the unexpected charges, lack of resolution, and the information I later received from my insurance company, this has been one of the most costly and frustrating healthcare experiences I’ve had. I am writing to document my experience with Alto Pharmacy and to share what I believe reflects unreasonable pricing practices and a failure to provide the most cost-effective option requested.

Timeline of Events

Before ordering my medications, I raised concerns about pricing with both my fertility clinic and Alto directly.

My nurse contacted Alto on my behalf to understand why the cost was so high and explicitly instructed them to provide the most cost-effective option available. This included switching from Follistim to Gonal-F if it was more affordable and applying all available discounts (including Maven, as I am a member).

Alto did not make this switch and did not present Gonal-F as an alternative, despite it being the more cost-effective option.

Instead, I was charged $4,430.60 for five days of medication:
-Menopur at $95 per vial
-Follistim at $868.90 per cartridge

I obtained a quote from a comparable pharmacy:
-Follistim at $168 per cartridge
-Menopur at $89.99 per vial

The price difference was $2,803.60 on Follistim alone.

Escalation Response

When I escalated this with Alto, I was told:

They “don’t do retroactive price matching” and that I should have contacted them before delivery, despite the fact that both my provider and I had already contacted Alto about pricing concerns in advance.

The other pharmacy “must be a specialty pharmacy working differently with insurance.” This was inaccurate, as I had no fertility medication coverage.

There was no documentation that my clinic had requested the most cost-effective option. That option would have been Gonal-F, which was priced at $247 per cartridge, and Maven discounts apply specifically to Gonal-F.

Over the course of two weeks, I repeatedly called and sent messages requesting escalation. I disputed the charge with my bank and involved a representative from Health Advocate to assist me. After all of this, Alto offered a $400 discount, which did not materially address the pricing difference. I paid the discounted invoice as it’s became clear that the escalations manager was not willing to take any form of accountability. I never sought to avoid payment; I was seeking transparency and appropriate pricing after raising concerns in advance.

This is not simply about price matching. It is about failing to offer the most affordable option after it was explicitly requested. I was told during my first call with the pharmacy escalations manager, Yvonne, that Gonal-F should have been offered to me as an alternative. As I have no other option, I am formally escalating this matter and pursuing all available remedies.

Fertility treatment is already emotionally and financially overwhelming. Patients rely on pharmacies for pricing transparency and accurate information. That did not occur in my experience, and I paid approximately $2,800 more than I would have at another pharmacy for the same medication.

I do not recommend Alto Pharmacy for fertility medications or for services where cost transparency is critical.

They also have their own line of beautiful products designed specifically for the Thompson Chemists that they are so proud of. This is just a few blocks from the CVS, so please opt for Thompson Chemists instead of you can :) And if I haven’t sold you yet, believe it or not they even host small bluegrass music nights the second Tuesday of every month. The staff is knowledgeable, friendly, and always willing to go the extra mile to make sure you get exactly what you need.

Not only do they provide top-tier pharmaceutical care, but they also carry the best selection of medical and compression stockings I’ve seen anywhere. Whether you need them for circulation, recovery, or comfort, they offer a wide range of brands, sizes, and styles and the staff is incredibly helpful when it comes to fittings and recommendations.

Around the middle of May, I came here to fill my SSRI prescription, which I’ve been taking for over five years. When I arrived, I was told they didn’t accept my insurance and that my prescription would need to be transferred to West Side Pharmacy. While I was understandably frustrated, I accepted that and was preparing to leave empty-handed. After the pharmacists went back and forth for several minutes, they told me they could fill it this one time, but that future refills would need to go through West Side.

Fast forward to today. I ran out of my medication around Wednesday of last week and I forgot to refill it before going out of town. By the time I returned, I had been without my medication for about five days and was experiencing significant withdrawal symptoms, including nausea, lightheadedness, and extreme emotional sensitivity.

I first tried filling my prescription at another pharmacy because I didn’t want to deal with the insurance issues here again. They told me they couldn’t fill it because it had already been processed at Park West. So I returned to Park West, where I was told I had received a 90-day supply back in May and wasn’t eligible for another refill.

I calmly explained that I believed I had only received a 30-day supply, but the staff repeatedly insisted that wasn’t possible. The two female pharmacists who had helped me during my original visit were both there and immediately shook their heads, making me feel like they assumed I was lying. I then waited over 25 minutes for the manager to come speak with me. Rather than trying to understand what might have happened, he also treated me as though I was being dishonest. He asked if I had my previous prescription bottle with me, which of course I didn’t—I wasn’t expecting to have to prove that I hadn’t been given the full quantity months earlier.

After going back and forth for quite some time, the manager finally gave me a bottle containing the remaining two months of medication, assuming that I had only received a 30-day supply initially. While I’m grateful I was able to get my medication, the entire interaction left me feeling completely dismissed and gaslighted.

When I got home, I even dug my old prescription bottle out of the trash because I felt like I was going crazy. The QTY on the bottle was 0, making me think it was a one-off smaller dosage since they were doing me a favor, rather than a QTY of 90. Seeing it helped reassure me that I hadn’t imagined the situation.

My advice: count your pills before you leave the pharmacy and double-check that you received the correct quantity. I have been a customer at Drug Mart for over 10 years and have spent tens of thousands of dollars over this period at this pharmacy during that time. Unfortunately, my last  interaction completely destroyed the trust I had in this place.

The day before my prescription was filled, the pharmacy actually called me, to go over my prescriptions being sent out the next day, and confirmed it would be same generic manufacturer I’ve been receiving as I’m sensitive to switching generics and have had bad reactions.

Despite that conversation, the prescription was filled incorrectly and delivered to me with the same manufacturer I sent back to them the month before.

When I called to explain that this had already been discussed and documented the day before and multiple times prior to that , the pharmacist got on the phone and told me he was “not dealing with this anymore to make 5 cents.”

After more than a decade of being a loyal customer, that level of disrespect was honestly shocking.

This wasn’t a complicated request — it had already been discussed, confirmed, and noted on my account before the prescription was filled. Instead of acknowledging the mistake, I was spoken to dismissively and made to feel like my business didn’t matter.

If this is how longtime customers are treated, I can’t recommend this pharmacy. I’ve already switched pharmacies and they’re happy to accommodate and work with me as a partner in managing my healthcare. As someone with crohnic health issues ( CML) having a good relationship with your pharmacy is just as important as good relationship with your oncologist.

I was almost hesitant to leave a review as I didn’t want to have others knowing about them.

All things aside from their customer service via phone, online and in person to getting prescriptions filled and ability to speak with front desk or pharmacy - it is the only pharmacy where I have not once left or hung up still confused, frustrated or annoyed.

Everyone is extremely friendly knowledgeable, transparent and organized. They will quickly connect you with correct person if they are not appropriate party to speak with. Everything is seamless and it honestly seems too good to be true. As I hope they’ll be able to stick to this high quality service as they grow.

When you call - there is never a hold time and if there is it’s a matter of seconds.

The store itself is easily located near my gym and is clean, relaxed and never a wait time. If so they have comfortable seating and seltzer or flat water for you to enjoy while waiting (max 5 minutes tops).

You can choose to have delivery or pick up depending on convenience to proximity of where you live.

The pharmacists understand various situations that are out of everyone’s control in terms of supply and demand. And personally work with you doing everything they can to fulfill your order.

While not family owned you get a family owned vibe or relationship from every level of staff who works there.

Ed and Mark are extremely friendly, work with you and will explain what’s going on with something, extremely transparent and friendly at the same time.

No one is trying to push you out the door or provide short confusing answers to your questions. Let alone look miserable working for the larger pharmacies as I’ve experienced at the two dominant pharmacies/stores that are on every block where volume not customer relationship is their priority and business model.

Highly highly recommend. The biggest highlight was the staff. The anesthesiologists were fantastic — they took time to explain the epidural, answered all my questions, and had excellent bedside manner. My delivery nurse was absolutely amazing and made the entire experience feel calm and supported.

Some things the hospital does really well:

• You can have two support people plus a doula
• The Northwell app lets you see medications, notes, and diagnoses in real time
• You can wear your own clothes during delivery
• Nitrous oxide is available as a pain option (though it’s still fairly new)
• The discharge education was excellent due specifically to Erin— they even helped ensure our car seat was safely installed
• The nursery was helpful when we needed rest and is fist come first serve
• Bella Photography took beautiful newborn photos in your recovery room and allowed you to bring props
• There’s a comfortable family room for visitors
The birth registration office was super helpful, they didn’t put any pressure on us because we were still deciding the name, we really appreciated that.

However, there were also some challenges:

• Triage felt outdated and the changing area lacked privacy and seating
• Delivery and recovery rooms are quite small with limited seating, having folding chairs
• The postpartum unit sometimes ran out of basic supplies (linens, blankets, disposable underwear, no shower chair)
• There were several instances where I requested medication or supplies and waited hours to receive it
• Breastfeeding support felt discouraging rather than supportive
• I was not offered a breast pump when told I wasn’t producing enough milk only told you use formula
• Food ordering required calling a number and sometimes waiting on hold (would be much easier through the app); the food was actually pretty good.

The patient transport elevator does not work properly, it took a really long time to move between floors and when discharged it took a very long time.

Overall, the clinical staff and delivery team were wonderful and made a huge difference in the experience. The nursing staff was hit or miss. With a few operational improvements — particularly around supplies, postpartum support, and responsiveness — this could easily be an even better experience for new families.

Tip of things to bring:
1. Compression socks for swelling
2. A donut pillow if you want to sit anywhere other than the bed
3. Sleeping bag for your support person
4. Adult diapers to go home if you have a long drive

The postpartum team, however, was a completely different experience. I’ve had children at another hospital before, so I do have something to compare this to.

The entire system felt designed to make rest impossible — or maybe there’s just a serious lack of common sense.

At 10 PM, a cleaning staff member came through the hallway banging, shouting, and slamming things around before entering our room to collect trash while we were asleep. The nurses and other staff weren’t much better. Different people kept coming into our room at all hours of the night, repeatedly waking both me and my wife during our two-night stay.

At one point around 4 AM, a young staff member tried to wake my wife up after she had finally fallen asleep. My wife told her she was exhausted and needed rest, and the response was: “That’s why I’m here — to wake you up,” said cheerfully.

As if that wasn’t enough, a hospital photographer knocked on our door asking if we had 20 minutes for photos. No, we didn’t. We wanted sleep. And every time someone came in uninvited, the baby woke up crying.

There’s no nursery, so the baby stays in the room with the parents the entire time. If that’s the setup, why make the environment so noisy and disruptive?

The most frustrating part was the formula policy. Every time we needed a bottle, we had to buzz for a nurse because they only allow one bottle at a time and require scanning our wristband. So every two hours, I had to call someone into the room just to feed my newborn — waking everyone up again in the process.

The whole experience was exhausting and honestly beyond ridiculous. Over a three-day stay, I probably got two hours of sleep total. I came into the ER and immediately received a bed. You can also check wait times for the ER on Langone's website.

I was impressed with the speed of everything in the ER. The ER was hectic and a little crowded but I was taken care of and able to get tests and imaging done quickly. I entered the ER around 7pm and was admitted after a few hours. At around 7am the next day I was transferred to a shared room at Tisch.
The level of care I received was exceptional. The diagnostic workup was thorough, ruling out every possible alternative diagnosis before treating me. The team anticipated complications before they happened and monitored intensively. After 5 days I was transferred to a private room in Kimmel, this is where the video on my review was taken. The room was big, bigger than the average NY apartment, cleaned daily, and had a great view of the city.

The nurses in both Tisch and Kimmel treated me with kindness and were genuinely friendly. The food was also pretty good and the croissants from the Kimmel dining hall were exceptional. All the doctors and nurses were responsive, knowledgeable, and genuinely invested in my recovery.

What impressed me most was the multidisciplinary approach. I had teams from gastroenterology, endocrinology, internal medicine, radiology, and pathology all coordinating my care simultaneously and it was seamless. I never felt like I was falling through the cracks despite having so many teams involved. Lab results, documents, and notes were all easily accesible via my iPhone on the NYU Langone app.

I'd like to give a special shoutout to nurses Eunice, Mikhail, Meghan, Hannah, Olivia, and Luis. Maya, a medical student working on my case. There are incredible doctors and nurses here at NYP Columbia, where I've been going for over five years.

However, I have had so many demoralizing experiences with their scheduling failures that I figured I would warn others.

I have been scheduled for multiple appointments the providers/radiologists weren't ready for -- and have therefore been sent home multiple times without being seen. 90 minutes each way, losing a whole day of work. This has DIRECTLY impacted my health multiple times.

If you need to use this hospital, you need to be a full time self advocate, even more than normal. You need to call ahead, a month before every appointment, and ask them IN DETAIL if they are ready to see you and have read your whole chart. Then, a week out, call again.

Over the years, I have visited this facility multiple times seeking medical care for my parents, siblings, and occasionally myself. However, due to repeated negative encounters with the front desk, medical staff, excessive wait times, and an overall lack of empathy and urgency, I have often avoided coming here for my own care.

Most recently, I arrived at the emergency department at 3:00 PM with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, concerned about a possible appendix-related issue—something that should not be ignored. The check-in process took an excessive amount of time, seemingly complicated by my TRICARE (military) insurance.

After approximately an hour, I was initially seen in fast track, where my vitals were taken and a urine sample was collected. However, after briefly hearing my symptoms, I was told they could not proceed with my care and was sent back to the waiting room. I then waited an additional two hours before being called again.

During the second evaluation, a nurse asked a few questions and directed me to another waiting area. A newly assigned nurse repeatedly asked me the same set of questions I had already answered multiple times, which reflected a lack of coordination and training.

Eventually, I was seen by a physician assistant who conducted a thorough evaluation. I appreciate his professionalism, as he asked appropriate questions and addressed my concerns effectively under the supervision of two physicians. Following the examination, I was informed that I would likely need blood work and a CT scan, and I was instructed to return to the waiting area.

After being called back again for the physicians to verify my symptoms before ordering the CT scan, I experienced the most difficult part of my visit. From approximately 8:17 PM to 1:58 AM, I waited for the CT scan. During this time, I remained seated in a chair with an IV line, experiencing ongoing abdominal pain, without being offered a bed, water, or food. The CT scan results did not come back in hours. The conditions were extremely uncomfortable and distressing.

It is concerning that patients are expected to endure 12–18 hours in the emergency department without adequate comfort or timely care. The facility consistently appears overcrowded, with insufficient space, poor cleanliness, and visible trash. Additionally, many staff interactions came across as dismissive and lacking compassion.

I hope this feedback highlights areas that require immediate attention, particularly regarding patient flow, staff training, adequate staffing,

Their care, compassion, and professionalism during such a difficult time did not go unnoticed, and my family is very grateful.

However, I also need to raise some serious concerns. When my family member was moved to the 10th floor, I was honestly in disbelief at the condition of the unit. There was a noticeable odor, and overall it felt like the area is in need of renovation and better upkeep.

Additionally, the cleanliness of the family lounge on the fifth floor has been very disappointing. I’ve been there for seven consecutive days, and on at least three of those days, there was no toilet paper in the bathroom. During his stay, he was first cared for in the ICU and later transferred to the regular unit, 9E, Bed 18B.

First, I would like to sincerely recognize the ICU team. The care my father received in the ICU was excellent. The doctors, nurses, and staff were attentive, professional, and compassionate. Our family truly appreciated the dedication and care they provided during such a difficult time.

I would especially like to express my deepest appreciation to Dr. Fox and Dr. Watanabe. They were incredibly attentive throughout my father’s hospitalization. They visited him every day, explained his condition and progress clearly, and always took the time to answer all of my questions. Their patience, kindness, and compassion gave our family comfort and reassurance. They treated my father with dignity, respect, and genuine care.

I would also like to recognize Nurse Danny Tran. Although he was not my father’s assigned nurse and was only covering breaks, every time he came to help, he showed extraordinary kindness, patience, and thoughtfulness. The care he provided truly stood out. He was extremely thorough when helping my father, making sure he was cleaned properly, changed comfortably, and cared for with great attention to detail. He carefully checked everything, never rushed, and made sure nothing was missed. His dedication, professionalism, and genuine compassion deeply touched our family.

I also want to acknowledge Nurses Sheti and Samira. They were both kind, helpful, and attentive. They checked on my father regularly, made sure he was comfortable, and responded to his needs with care. Their support meant a lot to our family.

At the same time, I would like to share some concerns about my father’s experience after he was transferred from the ICU to the regular unit. The level of care and environment felt very different compared with the ICU. During the 16 days he stayed in the regular unit, the room condition was often disappointing. The room was not kept as clean as we expected, and there was only one occasion when someone came to clean the floor during that entire period. For a patient recovering from a serious illness, maintaining a clean and comfortable environment is extremely important.

We also noticed that when my father pressed the call button for assistance, it sometimes took a long time for someone to respond. For patients who may be weak, unable to move easily, or in need of immediate help, timely response is very important for their safety and comfort.

I share this feedback because we truly appreciate the many wonderful healthcare workers who cared for my father, and we believe every patient deserves the same level of attention, cleanliness, and responsiveness throughout their entire hospital stay—not only in the ICU but also in the regular units.

Overall, we are extremely grateful to E 9th Fl Dr. Fox, Dr. Watanabe, Nurse Danny Tran, Nurse Sheti, Nurse Samira, Samtha and all the staff members who showed kindness and compassion toward my father. I can’t remember all the moves that she gave me to do, but she also emailed them to me, so I have them there if I want a refresher.

The location is pretty much like any other PT location, but the staff is really where they shine. And by staff, I mean Candace. She really paid attention to me, tried to coach me as best she could, and I’ve tried to take away as much as I could.

I have PT for my back coming up, I’m going to try and set it up with her as well. I may not remember everything, but really, I have it in my emails so I can get them anytime. The one major move that she gave me seems to be really helpful, retraction and extension. I do it every single day, several times a day along. This along with yoga and some other therapy movements seem to be helping me recover. Hopefully she can help me out with the back as well.

I really do need to look up and do those other moves she prescribed though. I’ve also updated my chair and pillow. The pillow is actually still an ongoing search, but I do have a front contender that might be it. I have also been trying to focus more heavily on my posture. That’s key in all this.

Recognition for Nurse Linda Voigt Toussaint, RN

My husband was recently rushed to the ER and later admitted. Despite the clear short‑staffing challenges, the team worked tirelessly to care for their patients. When he was transported to the 5th floor, I was exhausted, emotional, and vulnerable — and that’s when Nurse Linda Voigt Toussaint became the breath of fresh air we desperately needed.

Linda made us feel comfortable from the moment she entered the room. She was attentive, patient, and compassionate, answering every question and ensuring my husband received the best possible care. Throughout the night, she monitored him closely and consistently, never once making us feel like a burden.

Her professionalism, empathy, and integrity were evident in everything she did. It’s clear that caring and healing are truly her calling. After so many years in nursing, it’s inspiring to see that she has not become desensitized, but instead continues to provide outstanding, heartfelt care. She is without question an asset to this hospital.

Thank you, Linda. I wish every patient could experience the level of care you provide.

[{"Name":"P L","ProfilePicture":"https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/ALV-UjVxLpVzYv6bHVJV1XGpNErn3mGobDtMOInQGMrsc1SGypKv8lDQ=s120-c-rp-mo-ba12-br100","Rating":5,"Description":"Being it’s during COVID, there were minimal people at the ER Dept. I arrived, triage and into a bed very quickly to address my emergency situation. Note that there was only one person ahead of me when I arrived in the waiting area.
I was placed into an room with curtains as door and all the procedure was done very efficiently and was seen my a doctor very soon. The was very attentive, asked all the necessary question and address my concern effective. MRI was done and amazes me the advancement on medical tech. I did not need to get out of bed or move as they brought a portable X-ray machine to do my X-ray. I didn’t even have to move as they did everything whilst I was in bed. Absolutely awesome.
Eventually, I was administer for emergency surgery. I was brought up to my room. It wasn’t a shared room. I either was lucky or it’s the COVID protocol. The room was very clean, comfortable. Heated bathroom floor and even come with a toiletries kit that have sleep mask, ear plus, hair brush, body wash, shampoo, conditioner, body lotion and alcohol free mouth wash!
My bed was fully adjustable. The bed was like being on a Biz class seat on a plane but more comfortable and wider.
The nurses and pre-op team were all amazing. Especially double kudos to the whole nursing team as well as the patient services team and managers.
I am not sure if I got extra attention or it’s just how good they are. On the 1st night there was some difficulty in getting my med and possible confusion or communication error. It became a big issue that got elevated to the Chief of Operation on that shift due to an on duty doc not calling in my required med when needed rather he would do it the next morning. The whole debacle had patient services checkin in on me twice a day for the remaining 5 days I was there to make sure any needs is taken care off and expediently.
Regardless, I really appreciate the effort everyone took to make me feel comfortable.
Since there were a lot of staff that attended to me, and I was on heavy medication, I couldn’t remember everyone’s name. I will at my best name a few to say a huge thank you to them and those whose name is not listed below, know that you are included.
Thank you to Karla, Wanda, Jamel, Ogeeda, Patrick, Christina, Tanya Amanda, Andreater, Caroline (PT) the Patient Services, Anesthesia and PT team, David Paul, last but not least Dr. Brisson.

Heated bathroom floor and even come with a toiletries kit that have sleep mask, ear plus, hair brush, body wash, shampoo, conditioner, body lotion and alcohol free mouth wash!
My bed was fully adjustable. The bed was like being on a Biz class seat on a plane but more comfortable and wider.
The nurses and pre-op team were all amazing. Especially double kudos to the whole nursing team as well as the patient services team and managers.

The complaints arrive rapidly: filthy bathrooms, no toilet paper, no blankets, no quilts, dirty rooms, rude staff, no food, no updates, and a doctor who appeared six hours later for a thrilling six-minute guest performance. The most serious concern is that Taz says his diabetic wife, who also has high blood pressure, went sixteen hours without anyone checking her blood sugar or blood pressure. If accurate, that deserves a real explanation—not merely another staff member sighing dramatically and disappearing behind a curtain.

Then comes the review’s spectacular final act: the hospital placed a **male patient next to her**.

A man.

In a hospital.

Near a woman.

Taz investigated personally by walking around the department, locating what appeared to be “plenty of space,” and developing an immediate hospital-wide room reassignment plan. The review closes with the unforgettable declaration that Taz would not enter this hospital even after being shot directly across the street. To begin with, on each occasion, from the moment I tried to enter, I was courteously stopped and patted down by the female security guard who explained why an electronic scan was necessary after the alarm went off. Not many people were in the waiting room, so I was promptly processed and called into an inner office for further medical intake information, and my BP was taken and recorded.

I was then taken into a small waiting room where I could lie down and recline to my comfort, while multiple hospital personnel checked my BP from time to time. I even had a doctor come in and explain that my BP had come down to a manageable number and that an IV Infusion/Drip was no longer necessary.  Instead, I was given fresh prescriptions and directed to the on-site pharmacy, which they said “was more convenient than driving across town to Costco Pharmacy.”

After all of those experiences, I can say without hesitation that HSS has earned every bit of its outstanding reputation.

From the moment you walk through the doors, every member of the staff treats you with professionalism, kindness, and genuine compassion. The nurses, physician assistants, therapists, anesthesiologists, and support staff consistently go above and beyond to make what could be a stressful experience as comfortable as possible.

A special thank you to Dr. Thomas Sculco. His skill, knowledge, and bedside manner are second to none. He takes the time to listen, explain, and genuinely cares about his patients’ outcomes. My mom thought she had a stomach virus but she began having stomach pains that were increasing with severity so we had to call 911. Harlem Hospital was the closest so that’s where they took her. The check in was speedy and they immediately took her through triage. My mother’s pain level was so high they had to give her morphine just to examine her. The morphine put her in a sedated state while they ordered some tests. The nurse (She wears the Star Wars clogs) in charge of my mom seemed nice and compassionate at first. As the wait for the testing grew longer the morphine was starting to wear off.  When I initially told the nurse the pain was returning she said ok as if she would be in soon. I waited over 15 minutes before I asked her again. She said yes, she knew and she’d be with me shortly. The third time I asked she said the doctor wanted my mom to have the test first and I said I understood that but if the test wasn’t happening soon they couldn’t just leave my mom in pain.
She said she would see how many people were ahead but at this point she was speaking with an attitude and was unbothered by my concern for my mom.
I waited another 15 minutes before an LPN named Jenny came in to check on us. When I asked her about my mom’s test and her pain meds she stated sympathetically that the head nurse said we weren’t getting any meds. I became very upset and confronted the nurse about what was going to be done for my mom. That’s when she said radiology was ready for her. But clearly they weren’t because my mom was gone a long time and she told me when she came back that they had her waiting in the hallway awhile before they did the cat scan. All without any pain meds. Jenny came in and I told her we needed meds ASAP because at this time my mom is crying and screaming in pain.
The doctors came in and said they saw a blockage and she needed surgery. Then the head nurse came and said that's why they needed to wait to give meds, to make sure they weren’t causing more harm. BS, their triage had their share of homeless people and a few DHS agents there to get them out of the ER and into shelters. They probably thought my mom was another addict looking for a warm bed and a hit.
The doctor needed to insert a drainage tube down my mom's throat into her stomach. The drainage didn’t work and rather than checking it they just left it while they continued to come back and forth to discuss the surgery they were planning in the next 8 hrs. So after nine hours in the ER we get to the surgical floor and the nurse comes and hands me a crumpled sheet of paper to fill out. It’s the surgical floor intake form. All the questions are basics that should have been noted during her ER registration and accompanied her upstairs. But nope, she came up with no records, not even orders to keep her sedated. I told them I needed the social worker as soon as they arrived because we were transferring out. The room had five beds in it and I can only imagine how difficult it must be to recover from anything with the constant interruption of quietness  with five people in a room.
The staff adamantly tried to dissuade us from leaving but we demanded to be transferred to Weill-Cornell Hospital where her PCP was. I had to take my daughter to the psychologist after staying one night here. It's already stressful for my 7 year old daughter to have a procedure. This hospital made it worse. My daughter got a catheterization procedure in this hospital and stayed one night in the ICU. Doctor Holzer did a top notch procedure unlike the rest of the staff members. This one night in the ICU caused my child to have PTSD now.  She was crying and screaming about her eye after she came out from procedure. Her eye was in pain for almost 24 hours. In the ICU, the nurses and doctors were checking her eye and told me they found nothing. They told me they've never heard about eye pain after surgery. So, did they take this more seriously? Did they make sure the patient was fine after the procedure? The answer was no. They only gave her Acetaminophen and Morphine but the nurses didn't help much. Instead of having some rest after the procedure, she would fall asleep and wake up crying from eye pain every hour.  The nurses didn't seem to care much. While my child was crying and screaming for pain right in front of the nurse that was on the computer, I asked for ice packs for her eye pain. The nurse told me to wait 3 minutes and she never came back with any ice packs. I was getting very upset seeing that there wasn't any improvement in her eye pain. The next day I decided to take a look at her eye and found a scratch. She had a cornea abrasion from the procedure and it was never treated until I requested it. After being seen by a provider, there was no way to contact them directly to discuss adjusting my prescription dosage. Instead, I was told I would need to schedule and pay for another appointment simply to request a higher dose of a medication that had already been prescribed.

Then, the hospital main telephone number did not answer my calls, so I couldn't get routed to the appropriate phone number or desk.
Eventually, I went up to the main hospital location and was directed to the community health center, and I think I got the correct number. But, my calls in the middle of the business day were not answered (I had to leave a message with a person on an "overflow line") and I could not visit the lab in-person to make an appointment.
I cannot speak for any treatment here because I did not receive any yet, but it's clearly a disjointed and dysfunctional phone system that does not facilitate communication to schedule treatment.  The hospital system generally and departments specifically would be able to provide better care from the time of scheduling if they would tighten up and attend to their phone presence.

Update:
A call back from a scheduling assistant led to (a) no confirmation of receipt of lab order fax; (b) no promise of call back from someone else like a nurse practitioner who may have any knowledge of receipt of fax; and, (c) a push to have me and PCP start the cycle of referral all over again instead of the infusion lab even confirming receipt of a fax.  While I understand the limitations of roles and the division of labor in the system, it is becoming clear to me that here bureaucracy is more important patient care.
We'll see if I ever get a call back because the scheduler said she would make no promise.  In the meantime, because treatment can no longer wait, I have no choice but to see treatment elsewhere and in less convenient locations.
Downgrading from 2 stars to 1 star.

Update #2:
After having primary physician fax records and injection order again, I received no confirmation or call.  After several calls and multiple messages left (only with the overflow line; I have not been able to connect directly with someone in the infusion center  since my first contact), I still have yet to receive a call in return.  Until I receive a call back and a willingness to establish care, I have no choice but to feel that this facility does not want to establish or even administer care.

Update #3:
Finally heard back directly from someone in the infusion center and have an appointment scheduled. I eventually felt so confused and bad for frazzling her that I agreed to just do the regular routine bloodwork that day and skip the additional tests.

In order to get the results of my routine bloodwork from my physical, I was required to schedule a follow-up appointment, which will be billed as another visit. There is no patient portal or any other way to access your records.

With more time to think about it, I realized I was essentially being squeezed for more money. Our providers review labs and will contact a patient with normal unremarkable labs to cancel the appointment if there is nothing to discuss. After 20 years of serving busy New Yorkers who cannot answer their phones consistently, and who travel and move in and out of New York consistently, we have found dedicated lab review time for abnormal results is essential in making sure medical problems can be safely this is our best practice and its the health of our patients we are prioritizing with this approach to scheduling. 5. Unfortunately, this experience was not unusual. Chronic delays appear to be the norm. Being seen on time is the exception rather than the rule, despite patients being expected to adhere strictly to appointment times.

What concerns me most is the lack of professionalism, communication, and compassion shown toward a particularly vulnerable patient population. Spravato is prescribed to individuals struggling with severe depression, anxiety, trauma, and other serious conditions. Many of the individuals I interacted with identified themselves as interns or trainees. While everyone needs to learn, I was often left with the impression that there was insufficient supervision, communication, and accountability for a clinic administering specialized treatments to vulnerable patients.

I was also required to establish care with one of the clinic's physicians who I also believe is one of the owners. Despite being a patient for approximately a year, I have had absolutely no meaningful communication, follow-up, or outreach from that physician. If a clinic requires patients to establish care with a specific doctor, I believe patients should reasonably expect some degree of ongoing physician involvement, continuity of care, and oversight. Instead, my experience has been the exact opposite. Outside of the separate psychiatric check-ins required for Spravato treatment, I have felt largely left on my own and have seen no evidence of an active physician-patient relationship with the doctor I was required to establish care with. Given the nature of Spravato treatment and the vulnerability of the patients receiving it, I believe the issues described above warrant serious review and attention. Victoria Oliver, BSN, RN is an absolute gem. As an aesthetic injector she is incredibly professional, precise, and genuinely passionate about what she does. I very rarely write negative reviews and do not direct my frustration towards any of the individual staff members.

That said, the wait that I endured today was far longer than any office should tolerate. I had an appointment for 11:00am and wasn’t taken into an exam room until approximately 11:45am.

Around that time, the kind medical technician took my vitals and administered  COVID/FLU and Strep tests. I was told that a physician would be going over the results with me in no longer than 10 minutes.

After 30 minutes of no one checking on me, I asked a staff member if the clinic had forgotten about me. The staff member assured me that the physician was exceptionally busy and that they would be with me in just a few more minutes.

30 minutes later, still no doctor had arrived. Fed up, I told the medical technician that I would be leaving. He then told me that my results were negative. I waited in the exam room for an entire hour to have them tell me something that they were able to convey in five seconds.

I continue to feel terrible physically and am disappointed that I could not discuss it with a doctor — even though I paid my copay and waited far longer than anyone should. I do truly feel sick and will go to another facility if I have to — I just couldn’t stomach waiting indefinitely any longer.
